Ingratiate

in-GRAY-shee-ayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To ingratiate is to work intentionally to gain someone's favor or approval.

The new neighbor ingratiated himself with the block by fixing everyone's fences for free.

Worked Example

The new intern tried to ingratiate himself with the senior staff by remembering everyone's coffee order.

Memorizing everyone's coffee order to win their favor is exactly ingratiating.

How Ingratiate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

curry favor

curry favor: seek approval through flattery or effort

win over

win over: gain someone's approval or support

Antonyms

repel

repel: push away or cause someone to dislike you

How Strong Is It? — befriend → ingratiate → suck up to

befriend vs. ingratiate

befriend vs. ingratiate: Befriend simply means becoming someone's friend, with no implied strategy; ingratiate implies a intentional, sometimes calculated effort to be liked.

suck up to vs. ingratiate

suck up to vs. ingratiate: To suck up to someone is the same idea in casual slang, more openly critical in tone, while ingratiate is the plain-to-formal word for the same strategy.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — grati

root — grati: favor, grace (Latin (gratia))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ingratiate comes from Latin in- ('into') + gratia ('favor, grace') -- literally 'to bring oneself into favor.'

Use the root in a new word: grateful

Use the root in a new word: grateful: The same gratia root gives us the everyday word grateful, feeling thankful -- both words trace back to that same idea of favor or grace.

Root Check

Word Choice

Ingratiate is almost always used reflexively ("ingratiate himself/herself/oneself") and describes a sustained, intentional effort to win someone's approval, not a single kind gesture.
